clue.text: Ely desperately after pen to house college transport

indicators.note: acting desperately means acting wildly, so these letters are thrown into disorder
to house something is to give it shelter inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a Bic is a familiar make of ballpoint pen
the cathedral city, used for its letters
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A frantic resident of Ely needs some way of getting to college.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled Ely becomes YLE, which wraps round C, and the whole lot comes after the pen: BIC + Y(C)LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bicycle is a pedal vehicle, a common means of getting about, so it counts as transport.

clue.text: Lawyers' bill for drink

blocks.note: the Bar is the body of barristers, with the possessive S
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: The legal team's invoice for the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Barsac is a sweet white wine from the Bordeaux region, so it is a drink.

clue.text: Tester of prison work finally happy

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word, so only its last letter is kept

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison
OP is short for opus, a work
the last letter of happy

explanation.surface: A prison inspector is finally pleased with the inmates' work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tester' looks like an examiner, but it is an old word for the canopy over a four-poster bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A tester is the canopy above a bed, so the two words name the same overhead covering.

clue.text: Decoration designed for X?

indicators.note: something designed is planned and arranged, so the letters are laid out in a new pattern

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A medal or ornament designed in the shape of a cross.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like a cross-shaped decoration or a kiss, but it is the horizontal position on a graph; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: The x-value of a point on a graph is one of its coordinates, so X is an example of one.

clue.text: Cast use Queen Ursula's debut play

indicators.note: to cast is to throw, so the letters are tossed into a fresh order
a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter counts

blocks.note: taken as written for its letters
Q is the chess abbreviation for queen
the first letter of Ursula

explanation.surface: A director casts the queen's actress Ursula in her first stage role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like choosing actors, but it is the anagram signal working on use plus the two single letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Equus is Peter Shaffer's 1973 stage drama about a boy who blinds horses.

clue.text: Scotsman broken by onset of injury and hard suffering

indicators.note: something broken by another thing is split open with the other thing lodged in the gap
'onset of' keeps only the first letter of 'injury'

blocks.note: Angus is a stock Scottish man's name
the onset of a word is its first letter
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A Scot hurt in an accident is in great pain.
explanation.walkthrough: I splits ANGUS between U and S, then H goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Anguish is severe mental or physical pain, a direct synonym for suffering as a noun.

clue.text: True! Rambo's swimming trunks to be seen here

indicators.note: swimming suggests a blurred, moving state, so the letters swirl into another order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, ignoring the possessive S

explanation.surface: Confirmation that Rambo's swimwear is on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunks' looks like swimwear next to 'swimming', but it means tree trunks.
explanation.definitionFit: An arboretum is a botanical collection of trees, so tree trunks are what a visitor sees there.

clue.text: One's fitted in gun carriage

indicators.note: something fitted in is placed inside, so this piece goes within the other

blocks.note: first part of GAT, slang for a gun
I is the Roman numeral one; 's is 'is'
last letter of GAT, closing round the inserted piece

explanation.surface: A soldier's part is mounted on a gun carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gun carriage' reads as one military term, but it splits: gun is the wordplay, carriage the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Carriage can mean the way a person holds and moves their body, which is their gait.

clue.text: Denials about cigar butt being Cuban?

indicators.note: about can mean round in all directions, so the letters are turned into a new order
the butt of a cigar is its end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
the last letter of cigar

explanation.surface: Someone denies that the cigar stub is a Cuban.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuban' looks like a cigar beside 'cigar butt', but it means a person from Cuba; the question mark says it is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is an island nation, so a Cuban is an example of an islander.

clue.text: No puritan, involving fellow in theft

indicators.note: involving means including within, so the word for theft wraps round the other piece

blocks.note: first part of HEIST, a robbery
a don is a fellow of a university college
the rest of HEIST, closing round the inserted piece

explanation.surface: An unpuritanical person drags a companion into a robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: A fellow at Oxford or Cambridge is a don.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist pursues pleasure, the very opposite of a strait-laced puritan.

clue.text: Musical piece produced by new department's head in jumper

indicators.note: the head of a word is its leading letter, so only that one is kept
these pieces sit inside the word for the animal, which encloses them

blocks.note: first part of ROO, Australian slang for a kangaroo, a famous jumper
N is the abbreviation for new
the first letter of department
last letter of ROO, which closes round the inserted pair

explanation.surface: A tune is composed by a newcomer heading a department, while wearing a sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like a sweater, but it is the kangaroo, ROO, which holds N and D: RO(ND)O.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form in which a main theme keeps returning between contrasting sections.

clue.text: Burn wayward lazy daughter? Wild!

indicators.note: wayward means straying from the proper course, so these letters wander out of order

blocks.note: taken as written for its letters
idle means lazy
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent's exasperated verdict on a reckless, idle daughter: torch the lot, she's out of control!
explanation.definitionFit: Unbridled describes a horse without a bridle, hence anything unrestrained or wild.

clue.text: Sanctimonious little girl in car plant

indicators.note: the two short pieces sit inside the name of the vehicle

blocks.note: first part of ASTRA, a Vauxhall car model
pi is crossword-familiar slang for pious or sanctimonious
Di is a short form of Diana
the rest of ASTRA, closing round the inserted pieces

explanation.surface: A prim little girl sits in the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb (to hide something in the car), but it is the definition. The Astra is a Vauxhall hatchback.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspidistra is a hardy leafy houseplant, a fixture of Victorian parlours, so it is a plant.

clue.text: See 24 Down
One who works over the shop?

definitions.text: One who works over the shop?

blocks.clueFragment: One who works over the shop?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who lives in the flat above their own business

blocks.clueFragment: One who works over the shop?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a tradesman who paints lettering on the fascia above a shopfront

explanation.walkthrough: 'Living over the shop' is a stock phrase for residing above one's business, which steers away from someone painting the name above the door.
explanation.definitionFit: This tradesman paints names and lettering on boards, typically the fascia above a shop window.

clue.text: Winner shouts out 'There's no merit in it!'

definitions.note: the whole exclamation describes a state, which is the noun's sense

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A winner yells that the victory was undeserved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shouts out' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'out' is the anagram signal working on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Unworthiness is the quality of lacking merit or deserving no credit, which the exclamation describes.

clue.text: Book set in US city or miserable, dark state

indicators.note: something set in another thing is placed inside it
miserable suggests being in a wretched, broken state, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for book
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A novel set in a grim American city, or one in a gloomy country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US city' looks like a setting for the book, but its letters, with 'or', are the jumble that B goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscurity is darkness or dimness, literally a dark state.

clue.text: Singular Côte d'Ivoire architectural style – O! is lost; quite a blow

indicators.note: something lost goes missing, so the named letter drops out

blocks.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
CI is the international vehicle code for Côte d'Ivoire
rococo is the ornate 18th-century style
the letter itself, which is removed

explanation.surface: An exclamation over the loss of a distinctive Ivory Coast building style, a real setback.
explanation.walkthrough: One O comes out of ROCOCO to leave ROCCO. 'Blow' looks like a setback but means a wind.
explanation.definitionFit: The scirocco is a hot, strong Mediterranean wind from North Africa, quite a blow in the gale sense.

clue.text: Drink associated with railway in recent times

blocks.note: a latte is a milky coffee
RLY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Coffee has become linked with train travel lately.
explanation.definitionFit: Latterly is an adverb meaning recently or of late, so it can replace the phrase in a sentence.

clue.text: Admonition, it seems, about breaking into song

indicators.note: about can mean in a disordered state, all around, so the letters are moved round
breaking into something means forcing a way inside it, so one piece lodges within the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
a chant is a simple song or sung refrain

explanation.surface: A rebuke, apparently, for bursting into song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Chastisement is a scolding or reprimand, which is what an admonition is.

clue.text: See 24
Brummie's refusal to do a turn as the title character

indicators.note: doing a turn means rotating round, so the pieces are read the other way

blocks.note: the setter Brummie speaking of something belonging to himself says my
nope is an informal no

explanation.surface: A Birmingham man refuses to perform in the role of the lead character.
explanation.walkthrough: Brummie is the setter, so 'Brummie's' is 'my'; a Brummie is also a native of Birmingham, which is the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An eponym is the person a work is named after, so the title character of a novel such as Emma is one.

clue.text: Mechanical routine giving balls energy

blocks.note: balls is British slang for nonsense, as is rot
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A dull exercise routine handing out balls for energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like sports equipment but means nonsense, ROT.
explanation.definitionFit: Rote is learning or doing by mechanical repetition, as in learning by rote.

clue.text: Maybe London's joint originator of written work

definitions.note: authorship is the origin of a text rather than its originator, a loose fit

blocks.note: Jack London was an American novelist, so he is an example of an author, with the possessive
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Perhaps a hip joint in London, of all places, started a piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London' looks like the city, but it is the writer Jack London; 'Maybe' signals that he is just one example of an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Authorship means the origin or source of a piece of writing, its being written by someone.

clue.text: Basic construction by American-Africans

blocks.note: a hut is a simple, basic building
US stands for American, as in US politics

explanation.surface: A simple building put up by African-Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins 'American' and 'Africans' into one phrase in the surface, though they belong to different parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hutus are a people of Rwanda and Burundi in central Africa.

clue.text: Joins the performance of Tosca (teen night production)

indicators.note: a production is something put together or staged, so the letters are assembled anew

blocks.note: the opera title and the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Someone joins a staging of Puccini's opera put on as a teenagers' evening.
explanation.definitionFit: To get in on the act is an idiom for joining an activity, often to share its rewards.

clue.text: Dash, it's rough being an ambitious type!

indicators.note: rough means crude and unpolished, so these letters are knocked out of shape

blocks.note: to career is to rush along at speed, as to dash is
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation of annoyance at how hard it is to be ambitious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash' reads as a mild oath, but it is the verb meaning to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A careerist is someone mainly concerned with advancing their own career, an ambitious type.

clue.text: Mark 2?

blocks.note: surface reading: a second version, or the second chapter of St Mark's gospel
setter's reading: the American novelist's first name followed by an old word for two

explanation.walkthrough: The writer's pen name is also an archaic word meaning two, so the name itself reads as 'Mark two'.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain is an old word for a pair and the surname of Mark Twain, the author of Huckleberry Finn.

clue.text: Backing positive, steadfast youth leaders to undertake major journey

indicators.note: backing means moving in the rear direction, so the whole string is read from its end
leaders are the ones at the front, so only the opening letters count

blocks.note: yes is a positive answer
the opening letters of the two words
to do a task is to undertake it

explanation.surface: Supporting upbeat, loyal young leaders as they set off on a big expedition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like 'supporting', but it applies to every piece that follows, so the whole string turns round at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An odyssey is a long, eventful journey, named after the wanderings of Odysseus in Homer's epic.

clue.text: Level of society needing pluck to restrain a totalitarian leader

indicators.note: restraining something means holding it in, so the word for pluck goes round the rest
the leader of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: to strum is to pluck the strings of a guitar
taken as written
the first letter of totalitarian

explanation.surface: A social class that requires courage to hold back a dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pluck' looks like courage but is the guitarist's action.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratum is a layer, and figuratively a class or level within society.
